title: How do you handle request aggregation in an API Gateway when multiple services must be queried (parallel WebClient + `Mono.zip`)?
shortTitle: Handling request aggregation when multiple services must be queried

s1_definition.profdef: Request aggregation is when the gateway, in response to a single client call, queries several backend services and composes their responses into one payload. The efficient way to do this in a reactive Spring Cloud Gateway or Spring WebFlux service is to issue the downstream calls concurrently with a non-blocking `WebClient`, each returning a `Mono`, and then combine them with `Mono.zip`, which waits for all of them to complete and emits a tuple you map into a single aggregated response. This turns many client round trips into one, and runs the backend calls in parallel rather than one after another.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh asks the National Bank of India help desk for a complete summary: his account balance, his card status, and his recent payments. A slow clerk would walk to the accounts room, come back, then walk to the cards room, come back, then walk to the payments room, taking three trips end to end. A smart clerk instead sends three runners at the same time, one to each room, waits at the desk until all three return, and then staples their papers into one summary sheet for Rajesh. The gateway doing `Mono.zip` over three parallel `WebClient` calls is that smart clerk.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fire the downstream calls in parallel with non-blocking `WebClient`, combine them with `Mono.zip`, and the client gets one aggregated response in the time of the slowest single call, not the sum of all calls.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Request aggregation is when the gateway, in response to a single client call, queries several backend services and composes their responses into one payload. The efficient way to do this in a reactive Spring Cloud Gateway or Spring WebFlux service is to issue the downstream calls concurrently with a non-blocking `WebClient`, each returning a `Mono`, and then combine them with `Mono.zip`, which waits for all of them to complete and emits a tuple you map into a single aggregated response. This turns many client round trips into one, and runs the backend calls in parallel rather than one after another.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh asks the National Bank of India help desk for a complete summary: his account balance, his card status, and his recent payments. A slow clerk would walk to the accounts room, come back, then walk to the cards room, come back, then walk to the payments room, taking three trips end to end. A smart clerk instead sends three runners at the same time, one to each room, waits at the desk until all three return, and then staples their papers into one summary sheet for Rajesh. The gateway doing `Mono.zip` over three parallel `WebClient` calls is that smart clerk.

**One line to remember:** Fire the downstream calls in parallel with non-blocking `WebClient`, combine them with `Mono.zip`, and the client gets one aggregated response in the time of the slowest single call, not the sum of all calls.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem aggregation solves is the chatty client. A dashboard that needs account, card, and payment data would otherwise make three separate calls, each with its own latency, its own auth, and its own failure chance. Moving the aggregation into the gateway means the client makes one call and the gateway does the fan-out.

The wrong way to aggregate is sequentially and blocking. If you call the account service, block until it returns, then call the card service, block, then the payment service, the total time is the sum of all three latencies, and you also tie up a thread the whole time. On a reactive gateway this also defeats the entire non-blocking model.

The right way uses the reactive `WebClient`, which returns a `Mono` without blocking. You start all three calls so they run concurrently, then combine them. For example, `Mono<Account> account = webClient.get().uri("/accounts/{id}", id).retrieve().bodyToMono(Account.class)` gives you a lazy, non-blocking handle to the account call, and you build similar monos for card and payment.

`Mono.zip` is the combinator. It takes several monos and returns a single mono that completes only when all inputs complete, giving you a tuple of their results. For example, `Mono.zip(account, card, payment).map(t -> new Dashboard(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3()))` produces one `Dashboard` object once all three downstream calls finish. Because the three monos were all subscribed concurrently, the total time is roughly the slowest single call, not the sum.

Error handling is the heart of a production aggregation. By default `Mono.zip` fails as soon as any input fails, so one dead service blanks the whole dashboard. Usually that is not what you want. You attach resilience to each individual mono so a failure degrades gracefully instead of killing the aggregate. For example, `card.timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)).onErrorReturn(Card.unavailable())` means if the card service is slow or down, that part of the dashboard shows "unavailable" while account and payment still render. Each downstream call also gets its own timeout, so one slow service cannot hold up the whole response.

For a variable or large number of downstream calls, `Flux.merge` or `Flux` with `flatMap` and a bounded concurrency is better than a fixed `Mono.zip`, because `zip` is for a known, fixed set of inputs. And for repeated identical sub-requests you cache results so the fan-out is cheaper.

A senior nuance is deciding where aggregation belongs. Simple view composition for a specific client fits the gateway, especially as a Backend-for-Frontend. But heavy aggregation with business rules should live in a dedicated composition service, not the gateway, so the gateway stays thin. Another nuance is partial-response semantics: you must decide and document whether the aggregated response is all-or-nothing or returns best-effort data with per-section status, and in banking, explicit per-section status is usually safer.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India mobile app shows Rajesh a home dashboard that needs three pieces of data owned by three different services: his account summary from the Account Service, his card status from the Card Service, and his recent payments from the Payment Service. If the app calls all three itself, the home screen is slow and the app is tightly coupled to three internal addresses. The gateway should aggregate.

Problem 2 — If the gateway calls the three services one after another, the dashboard is as slow as the three latencies added up, and if the card service is briefly down, a naive aggregation would blank the entire dashboard even though account and payment data are fine. We need parallel calls and graceful partial responses.

The connection to the fix: we will build an aggregation that issues three concurrent non-blocking calls and zips them into one dashboard. Each call has its own timeout and its own fallback, so the dashboard degrades gracefully. We will show both the all-success case and a case where the card service is down.

What the code will do. Because a runnable demo should not require a live reactive stack, we simulate the reactive pattern with `CompletableFuture`, which gives the same concurrent fan-out and combine semantics as `WebClient` plus `Mono.zip`, and we clearly comment where the real reactive equivalents go. There are three clients: `AccountClient`, `CardClient`, and `PaymentClient`, each with artificial latency and a toggle to simulate failure. There is a `DashboardAggregator` that fires all three concurrently, applies a per-call timeout and fallback, and combines them into a `Dashboard`. The demo runs the all-healthy case and the card-down case, logging total elapsed time.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is one request for Rajesh's dashboard for account SAV2001, handled twice: once with all services healthy, once with the card service down.

Step 1. The aggregator starts all three calls at the same time. The account call begins its 120-millisecond work, the card call its 100 milliseconds, and the payment call its 140 milliseconds, all running concurrently on the thread pool. This is the fan-out, the same thing subscribing to three monos does.

Step 2. Because the calls run in parallel, the aggregator is not waiting one-at-a-time. The card call finishes first at about 100 milliseconds, the account call at about 120, and the payment call last at about 140. The combine step, like `Mono.zip`, waits until all three are done.

Step 3. Once all three complete, the aggregator builds one `Dashboard` from the three results and returns it. The total elapsed time is about 140 milliseconds, the slowest single call, not 360 milliseconds, which is what sequential calls would have cost.

Step 4. In the card-down run, the card call throws. Its per-call fallback catches the failure and substitutes "Card unavailable", while the account and payment calls succeed normally. The combine step still completes because no mono failed the whole zip; the card part simply carries the fallback value.

Step 5. The returned dashboard in the second run shows the real account and payment data with the card section marked unavailable. The client gets a useful, mostly-complete screen instead of a blank error, which is the graceful partial-response behavior we wanted.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Request aggregation is when the gateway responds to a single client call by querying several backend services and composing their answers into one payload. The whole point is to turn a chatty client, which would otherwise make many round trips, into one call, and to do the backend work in parallel. In a reactive Spring Cloud Gateway or WebFlux service, the tool for this is the non-blocking `WebClient` combined with `Mono.zip`.

The key is concurrency. The wrong way is to call the account service, block until it returns, then the card service, block, then the payment service, because then the total time is the sum of all three latencies and you tie up a thread the whole time. The right way is to start all three `WebClient` calls so they run at the same time, each giving back a `Mono`, and then combine them with `Mono.zip`, which completes only when all of them complete and hands me a tuple I map into one response object. Because the three calls overlapped, the total time is roughly the slowest single call, not the sum.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, the mobile home dashboard needs three things owned by three services: the account summary, the card status, and the recent payments. The gateway aggregates them, so the app makes one call and gets one dashboard. The part that makes it production-grade is per-call resilience. By default `Mono.zip` fails the whole thing if any single call fails, which would blank the dashboard if the card service hiccuped. So I give each downstream call its own timeout and its own fallback, for example the card call falls back to an "unavailable" marker, so the account and payment sections still render while the card section degrades gracefully. That is the difference between a blank error screen and a useful, mostly-complete dashboard.

The nuances I always mention are two. First, `Mono.zip` is for a fixed, known set of calls; when the number of downstream calls is variable or large, I use a `Flux` with `flatMap` and a bounded concurrency instead. Second, I keep aggregation simple and view-oriented at the gateway, ideally as a Backend-for-Frontend, because heavy aggregation with real business rules belongs in a dedicated composition service, not the gateway, so the gateway stays thin and never turns into a hidden monolith. And I always decide explicitly whether the aggregate is all-or-nothing or best-effort with per-section status, and in banking I prefer explicit per-section status.
